ratings.description: Full credit: All four aspects described with accurate detail. No significant factual errors.
Partial credit: Most aspects described; one or two details missing or vague. Minor inaccuracy acceptable.
No credit: Little accurate description; major gaps or significant errors.
Full credit: Comparison is specific, accurate, and shows understanding of both the world tradition and the Music Theory I concept.
Partial credit: Comparison is present but vague or shows partial understanding of one side.
No credit: Comparison is missing or shows no understanding of the concepts being compared.
Full credit: Writing is specific throughout. Musical terms are used correctly. A reader unfamiliar with the tradition could follow the description.
Partial credit: Writing is mostly clear. One or two vague passages. Terms mostly correct.
No credit: Writing is too vague to evaluate the musical content. Terms missing or consistently misused.
Full credit: Reflection names a specific, genuine uncertainty and articulates what would be needed to resolve it.
Partial credit: Reflection is present but generic ("I could learn more") without specifying what is uncertain.
No credit: Reflection is missing or claims full understanding with no genuine engagement.

rubrics.title: Q4 Composition and Analysis Project Rubric

ratings.description: Full: Accurate use of 2 or more concepts; Beethoven key, chords, texture correct with measures.
Partial: Mostly correct; one or two errors.
Minimal: Significant errors; inconsistent.
None: Absent, plagiarized, or no engagement.
Full: Chart matches score; note explains why; Beethoven cites measures; log names two changes and defends one choice.
Partial: Present but underdeveloped.
Minimal: Vague; log missing or no changes.
None: Nothing submitted or generic.
Full: Clean score (clef, key, time signature, barlines, stems); precise note; accurate labels.
Partial: A few errors; some imprecision.
Minimal: Many errors; unclear.
None: Illegible or missing.
Full: Names something difficult or uncertain and what you tried. Honest uncertainty is credited.
Partial: Difficulty mentioned in passing.
Minimal: Claims everything worked.
None: No reflection, or copied.
3 points: Accurate, specific understanding.
2 points: General; minor inaccuracies.
1 points: Partial; key terms misapplied.
0 points: Missing or major misunderstanding.
3 points: Clear, specific case for your choices.
2 points: Present but general.
1 points: Thin; summary, not analysis.
0 points: None.
3 points: Clear ideas; precise vocabulary.
2 points: Mostly clear; some imprecision.
1 points: Unclear in places.
0 points: Unclear throughout.
3 points: Names what you understand well and where real gaps or questions remain.
2 points: Some uncertainty; mostly positive.
1 points: Generic; avoids real gaps.
0 points: Absent or performative.

questions.text: Essential question: How can a musician hear music before singing a single note? First answer, 2-3 sentences.

This module I will learn to: (a) define sight-singing and explain its importance, (b) understand movable-do solfege and scale degrees, (c) sing a melody using solfege syllables, (d) describe Curwen-Kodaly hand signs, (e) apply the five-step sight-singing strategy. Essential question: How do musicians write down what they hear? First answer, 2-3 sentences.

questions.text: In compound meter, the beat divides into:

An impression of a new key

Essential question: What makes the dominant seventh chord the most powerful chord in music? First answer, 2-3 sentences.

This module I will learn to: (a) define a seventh chord as a four-note chord built in thirds, (b) identify the five seventh chord qualities, (c) build any seventh chord quality above a given root, (d) identify seventh chords in notation, (e) recognize V7 as the most important seventh chord. Check that you have seen these goals.
How familiar are you with seventh chords right now?
A seventh chord is built by stacking a third above a:

The dominant seventh chord has which combination?
On which scale degree is the dominant seventh (V7) built?
A ma7 chord (major-major seventh) sounds:
A fully diminished seventh (o7) stacks all:
In C major, what are the four notes of G7?
The most dissonant interval inside a V7 chord, which drives its resolution, is the:
In a major key, which Roman numeral produces a half-diminished seventh chord?
The motion V7 to I is described as:

answers.text: the most powerful authentic cadence resolution in tonal music

Which seventh chord quality is hardest to remember? Describe what specifically is confusing.

In this module I will learn to: (a) define tonicization and contrast it with modulation; (b) identify secondary dominants using V/X notation; (c) recognize a secondary dominant by its chromatic note; (d) analyze a progression that includes V/V. Select "I have read these goals" to continue.
How confident are you right now with Roman numeral analysis of diatonic chords? (1 = not yet confident / 5 = very confident)
Tonicization is best described as...

answers.text: a permanent change of key that lasts for an entire section
using a chord from a different mode in the current key
a brief, temporary treatment of a non-tonic chord as a local tonic
the use of chromatic passing notes between two chords

questions.text: The notation V/V is read as...
In C major, V/V is...
How can you recognize a secondary dominant in a chord progression?

answers.text: It is always the chord immediately before the tonic
It always appears at the end of a phrase
It contains at least one chromatic note (a note not in the key signature)
It is always a diminished chord

questions.text: V/IV in C major resolves to...
Which interval separates a secondary dominant from its target chord?

answers.text: F-sharp (already in G major, not chromatic)

questions.text: How is tonicization different from full modulation?

answers.text: Tonicization is longer and establishes a new tonic for many measures
Tonicization only happens in minor keys
Modulation uses secondary dominants; tonicization does not
Tonicization is brief (1-2 chords); modulation is an extended change of key

questions.text: The progression I - V/V - V - I is notable because...

answers.text: it modulates to the dominant key permanently
it includes a secondary dominant that intensifies the approach to V
it uses only diatonic chords with no accidentals
it is an example of parallel motion in the bass

questions.text: In C major, V/vi resolves to...

Which step in identifying a secondary dominant is still hardest: spotting the accidental, dropping down a fifth to the target, or deciding on the V/X label? Name it.

This module rewards intellectual honesty: secondary dominants break the "rules" of the key temporarily, but in a controlled way. How does that connect to the virtue of integrity (acting by principle even when the rules are bent)?

Essential question: Where did the "rules" of music theory come from? Who decided how chords should move and how notes should resolve? Write 2-3 sentences. There is no wrong answer; this is your starting point.

In this module I will learn to: (a) define the Baroque period and name its approximate dates; (b) describe terraced dynamics, ornamentation, counterpoint, and the doctrine of affections; (c) explain basso continuo and figured bass; (d) name major works by J.S. Bach; (e) identify why Bach's chorales matter for music theory. Select "I have read these goals" to continue.
How familiar are you with Baroque music (any composers, any pieces) right now? (1 = never heard of it / 5 = I know it well)
The Baroque period in Western music is approximately...
Terraced dynamics means...

answers.text: sudden shifts between loud and soft sections
playing all notes at the same volume
dynamics that follow the natural rhythm of speech

questions.text: Which instrument's limitations explain why Baroque composers used terraced dynamics?
Counterpoint is defined as...

answers.text: one melody supported by chordal accompaniment
two or more independent melodic voices moving simultaneously
a bass line with figured bass numbers

questions.text: The doctrine of affections held that a piece of music should...

answers.text: use at least three different time signatures
include both major and minor sections
express a single unified emotion throughout
always end on a perfect authentic cadence

questions.text: In basso continuo, the figured bass numbers tell the chord player...

answers.text: which notes to add in the melody
which intervals to play above the bass note

questions.text: J.S. Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier consists of...

answers.text: six cello suites in six different keys
the Mass in B minor and the St. Matthew Passion
48 preludes and fugues, one in every major and minor key
over 200 church cantatas for choir and orchestra

questions.text: Why are Bach's four-part chorales important for music theory students?

answers.text: They use a different tuning system from other Baroque music
They are the only Baroque works that use figured bass
They are written for solo harpsichord with no other instruments
They provide a complete example of tonal voice leading, harmonic function, and cadence types

questions.text: The basso continuo ensemble texture includes...

answers.text: a solo singer and a piano
a bass instrument playing a bass line and a chord instrument improvising above it
four equal voices moving in counterpoint
a full orchestra with a conductor

questions.text: Which of the following is a correct description of ornamentation in Baroque music?

answers.text: A gradual increase in tempo toward the end of a phrase
The use of multiple time signatures in one piece
Decorative additions such as trills, mordents, and turns added to melodic lines
The practice of repeating the entire piece at a softer dynamic

questions.text: Essential question revisited: Now that you have studied the Baroque period, where do you think the rules of music theory actually came from? Who decided? Was it one person, one era, or a gradual process? Revise your original answer.
How confident are you describing at least two Baroque characteristics and explaining basso continuo? (1 = still not sure / 5 = I can explain it clearly)
Which Baroque concept is still least clear to you: terraced dynamics, counterpoint, basso continuo, or the doctrine of affections? Name it.

Bach composed over 1,000 works across his lifetime, often under demanding court and church schedules. How does that connect to the virtue of diligence? Describe one thing you can take from his example.

Essential question: When you listen to music, how do you know when a section feels like it is "arriving" or "coming home"? Describe that experience in 2-3 sentences. There is no wrong answer; this is your starting point.

In this module I will learn to: (a) define the Classical period and contrast it with Baroque style; (b) identify Classical features including homophony, balanced phrases, and gradual dynamics; (c) describe the three sections of sonata form; (d) describe contributions of Haydn and Mozart. Select "I have read these goals" to continue.
How familiar are you with the names Haydn or Mozart right now? (1 = I have heard the names but know little / 5 = I know their music well)
The Classical period in Western music is approximately...
Homophony is a musical texture in which...

answers.text: all voices move in identical rhythm
one melody is supported by accompanying harmonies
there is no accompaniment at all

questions.text: Classical phrase structure is typically...

answers.text: continuous and unbroken for long stretches
organized in balanced groups of 4+4 or 8+8 measures
built on a repeating ground bass

questions.text: The instrument that enabled gradual dynamics in the Classical era was...
In sonata form, the three sections in order are...
In a major-key Classical sonata, the secondary theme in the Exposition is typically in the...
The Development section of sonata form is best described as...

answers.text: a full restatement of both themes in the tonic key
a slow introduction to the main themes
a stable section in the subdominant key
an unstable exploration of themes through different keys

questions.text: What makes the Recapitulation sound like "coming home"?

answers.text: The primary theme returns at a faster tempo
The secondary theme now appears in the tonic key instead of the dominant
A new theme is introduced for the first time

questions.text: Joseph Haydn is best known for developing which two major musical forms?

answers.text: The symphony and the string quartet
The opera and the concerto grosso

questions.text: Which statement about Mozart is accurate?

answers.text: He composed primarily sacred choral music and wrote no operas
He was active primarily in the Baroque era, before Haydn
He began performing publicly at age six as a child prodigy
He wrote 104 symphonies over a long court career

questions.text: Essential question revisited: Now that you know sonata form, describe the "coming home" feeling in musical terms: what is actually happening harmonically when the Recapitulation arrives? Revise your original answer.
How confident are you naming the three sections of sonata form and explaining what happens in each? (1 = still unclear / 5 = I can describe all three from memory)
Which is still hardest for you: telling the Exposition from the Recapitulation by ear, understanding why the secondary theme's key matters, or distinguishing Classical from Baroque texture? Name it.
Mozart compressed extraordinary musical achievement into 35 years of life. How does that connect to the virtue of excellence (making the most of the time and gifts you have)? Write 1-2 sentences.
Essential question: When is breaking the rules of a style the right choice for a composer, and when is it just chaos? First answer, 2-3 sentences.
This module I will learn to (a) define the Romantic period, (b) identify key Romantic style features, (c) explain Beethoven's role as a bridge — check that you have seen these goals.
How familiar are you with the music of the Romantic period (roughly 1820-1900)?
The Romantic period in Western music spans approximately:
Which feature is NOT primarily associated with the Romantic period?
Beethoven's Third Symphony, the "Eroica," is significant because:

answers.text: it is widely considered the beginning of the Romantic era
it was composed while Beethoven could still hear perfectly
it introduced the symphony as a form

questions.text: A symphonic poem is best described as:

answers.text: a song for voice and piano
a multi-movement work for string quartet
a single-movement orchestral piece inspired by a literary or visual subject

questions.text: The term "lieder" refers to:

answers.text: a form of instrumental program music

questions.text: Program music is:

answers.text: purely abstract music with no extramusical reference
instrumental music that depicts a story, scene, or emotion
music written for a specific political program

questions.text: Which composer is primarily associated with transforming opera into "music drama" with revolutionary harmonic language?

answers.text: frequent use of notes and chords outside the current key
the use of chromatic tuners in performance

questions.text: Beethoven's Ninth Symphony is notable partly because:

answers.text: it was composed when Beethoven was completely deaf and includes a choral finale
it was composed in the Baroque style

questions.text: Which Romantic composer wrote primarily for solo piano, producing nocturnes, etudes, and mazurkas?

answers.text: a melodic mode in Arabic music that includes specific pitches, ornaments, emotional character, and performance conventions

answers.text: All notes are played twice as fast.

Notes are played exactly as written with no variation

It shows only the drum part

questions.text: The antecedent phrase ends on:
